newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, US still far apart over insurance issue--MOF.
newsitem.headline: Japan, US still far apart over insurance issue--MOF.

text.p: Japan and the United States are still far from reaching an agreement over their bilateral insurance dispute after two days of meetings between senior officials, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official told reporters on Monday.
Japan and the United States have been in negotiations since last week to resolve their insurance dispute before a self-imposed December 15 deadline.

The official said Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance Bureau, and United States Trade Representative (USTR) negotiator Ira Shapiro will meet again on Thursday and Friday before a ministerial meeting scheduled for Saturday.

Sakakibara and Shapiro held two days of talks on Sunday and Monday after Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and acting USTR Charlene Barshefsky failed to bridge their differences over the insurance trade issue in their latest round of talks last week.
"We have deepened our understanding of each other's position, but differences that the ministers could not narrow in their latest talks still exist," the official said.
"Negotiations are going to be very hard," he said.
The disagreement centres on U.S. charges that Japan is planning to renege on a 1994 trade agreement on the deregulation of its lucrative insurance market.

Washington has argued that the agreement calls for Tokyo to deregulate the huge primary life and casualty insurance sector, which is dominated by Japanese companies, before unleashing competition in the tiny specialty insurance market.
The niche market is the only one in which foreign insurance groups have a firm foothold.

The MOF official said Japan has made "drastic" proposals to liberalise its primary life and casualty insurance sector, based on the spirit of the "Big Bang" financial reforms to implement substantial deregulation by 2001, mapped out by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto recently.
